entries.definition: One of the skills the exam measures. Language has six that count: AO1, finding and interpreting information; AO2, analysing language and structure; AO3, comparing writers' perspectives; AO4, evaluating a text; AO5, writing content and organisation; AO6, technical accuracy. Each reading question assesses one of them and the writing question two, and the number is printed in the mark scheme, not on the paper.
entries.example: Paper 1 Question 2 is AO2 and Question 4 is AO4, so a Question 4 answer that only analyses language has answered the wrong objective.

entries.definition: How AQA marks the reading and writing questions: the whole answer is placed in a level by its overall quality, then given a mark within it. The reading questions have four levels; Level 4 is described as perceptive and detailed, Level 3 as clear and relevant, Level 2 as some understanding and comment, Level 1 as simple and limited.
entries.example: On Question 2, worth 8 marks, Level 4 is 7 to 8 and asks for analysis of the effects of the writer's choices, judicious detail and sophisticated, accurate terminology.

entries.definition: The mark scheme's example of what a response at each level looks like, written on the actual source. It is not a model answer and not a checklist; it shows the standard, and the same detail is often taken up a level at a time to show what deeper analysis adds.
entries.example: In June 2024 the scheme showed one simile, the lizards darting over the rocks like flames, commented on at Level 1, 2, 3 and 4, so that the difference between the levels was visible on one detail.

entries.definition: Chosen with judgement. The Level 4 descriptors for Questions 2 and 3 ask for a range of judicious textual detail or examples: the details that best answer the question and that connect with one another, not the first three things found or one quotation from every line.
entries.example: For a question on how the writer shows a character's feelings about her fur, the fur's dim little eyes and the exclamation over it are a judicious pair, because both make the fur a companion.

entries.definition: The shapes of sentences a writer chooses: long and winding, short and plain, a question, an exclamation, a list, a sentence that corrects itself with dashes. The third bullet under Question 2 names them, and they are a choice like any other, to be named and given an effect.
entries.example: In the opening of Miss Brill the exclamation Little rogue! lets the character's own voice break into the narration, and a sentence that changes its mind mid-way, sad, no, not sad, exactly, shows a feeling being adjusted as it is felt.

entries.definition: Third-person narration that takes on a character's own voice and thoughts without quotation marks or a he thought, so the reader is inside the character while the narrator keeps telling the story.
entries.example: Dear little thing! in the opening of Miss Brill is Miss Brill's own voice inside the narration: nobody says it aloud, and the narrator does not report it as a thought, yet the reader hears her.

entries.definition: Giving an object, an animal or an idea the qualities of a person. It earns marks in an answer when its effect is explained, not when it is merely spotted.
entries.example: Miss Brill's fur has dim little eyes into which she rubs the life back, and it asks What has been happening to me?: the personification makes the fur a companion, which tells the reader how little else she has to talk to.

entries.definition: A comparison made with like or as. The commonest technique students name, and the one most often named without an effect; the mark is for what the comparison brings with it.
entries.example: The conductor flapped his arms like a rooster about to crow: the simile makes him faintly comic and self-important, seen through the eyes of a woman who enjoys watching people, so it characterises the watcher as much as the man.

entries.definition: The shape of a whole text: what it focuses on first, how and why the focus moves, how time passes, whose perspective the reader shares, and how the ending sits against the opening. Question 3 asks about it, and the mark scheme names features at whole-text, paragraph and sentence level.
entries.example: Miss Brill opens with the fur coming out of its box, widens to the crowd and the idea of the play, turns on the young couple's words, and ends with the fur going back into the box: a cyclical structure whose return carries what the story never states.

entries.definition: The part of an opening that establishes setting, character and situation, and so sets what the reader watches for. The first bullet under Question 3 asks what the writer focuses attention on at the beginning, which is a question about exposition and expectation.
entries.example: The June 2024 source began with the heat suddenly becoming intolerable, exposition that put the character already at breaking point so that the reader expected her to snap.

entries.definition: A movement of the text's attention: from outside to inside, from wide to close, from one time to another, from description to a character's thoughts, from one voice to another. Naming a shift earns when its reason and its effect on the reader are given.
entries.example: In Miss Brill the reader has the character's own thoughts for most of the story; the shift to the young couple's dialogue is the only view of her from outside, and the story turns there.

entries.definition: Whose eyes and thoughts the reader is given. First person tells the story as I; third person can stay outside every character or stay close to one, sharing their thoughts. The choice decides what the reader knows and when, so it is a structural feature.
entries.example: The June 2024 mark scheme listed the source's third-person narrative as a structural feature because it allowed a switch between external description and the internal thoughts of both characters.

entries.definition: A shape in which the ending returns to the opening, changed. The return makes the reader compare the two moments and see what the text has done between them.
entries.example: Miss Brill takes the fur out of its box in the first paragraph and puts it back in the last, and when the lid goes on she thinks she hears something crying: the return carries the meaning the story never states.

entries.definition: An expectation raised and then allowed to drop, or a pay-off withheld. The June 2024 mark scheme named an anti-climax in its source, an expected argument that subsides when a character apologises. The opposite move, a habit set up so that its breaking can be felt, works the same way in reverse.
entries.example: Miss Brill is told that on her way home she usually buys a slice of honey-cake, so that the next paragraph, in which she passes the baker's by, is felt as a loss without being explained.
